newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss watch exports show shift to pricier models.
newsitem.headline: Swiss watch exports show shift to pricier models.

text.p: Latest Swiss watch export figures released on Thursday confirmed a trend towards pricier, more durable models, including timepieces made of steel, and away from plastic watches.
The industry also appears to be doing better overall according to the data published by the Federation of the Swiss Watch Industry.
In value terms, exports of Swiss watches rose 7.8 percent in the first half of 1997 to 3.857 billion Swiss francs ($2.6 billion) from 3.577 billion in the 1996 first half.
But in the same period, the number of individual finished watches exported fell 11 percent to 14.9 million from 16.7 million.

The Federation said the drop in export volume was mainly due to declines in exports of plastic wristwatches, which fell 25.5 percent in the first half of 1997. This decline was offset only partly by a gain in volume exports of watches made of other, more expensive materials such as gold and steel.
Steel-watch exports rose 10.4 percent in volume terms, and by 32.8 percent in terms of value.
The Federation said sales were helped by weakness in the Swiss franc versus the U.S. dollar, and by improved business in two major European export markets, Germany and Italy.
Ueli Trachsel, director of finance at TAG Heuer International SA, said the latest statistics "are giving some signals. Overall I would say it (the report) confirms the trend."
Trachsel was unwilling to detail sales at TAG Heuer before release of its half-year results on Friday.
"Mainly I would say we can confirm more or less these figures as they are," he said of the export data.
But, he added the export data are not final sales numbers, and "what counts are local sales in respective countries."

Regarding the trend showing declines in exports of plastic watches, Trachsel said: "If you buy a plastic watch, the next day the model has already changed. It is somehow no longer the style of the current generation. They would like to live with it (a watch) for a long time. The trend has changed, the consumer wants to have a well-positioned product with a certain image."
TAG Heuer does not make plastic watches, and is strongly promoting its higher-priced steel and gold brands.
Ste Suisse Microelectronique et d'Horlogerie SA (SMH) has also had good success with its new "Irony" steel-watch brand, say analysts.

SMH's president Nicolas Hayek is credited with helping to save the Swiss watch industry in the 1980s with his successful marketing of the firm's plastic "Swatch" watches, still the dominant plastic Swiss watch brand.
Frederick Hasslauer, analyst at Bank Sal. Oppenheim jr & Cie, said that the success in SMH's steel-watch sales now may in fact be undercutting its plastic-watch sales.
Referring to the latest figures, he estimated that roughly half of the increase in exports in value terms in the first half of 1997 was tied to the weaker franc, which boosted the reported value.
Hasslauer is also generally optimistic about the industry.
"Encouraged by the weakening of the Swiss franc, it appears Swiss watch exports are continuing the recovery seen in the fourth quarter of 1996," he said.
-- Zurich Editorial, +41 1 631 7340 ($ = 1.509 Swiss Francs)
